title: Elizabethtown from Severns Valley
summary: Before Elizabethtown there was Severns Valley, settled in spring 1780 by families who guarded it with a defensive triangle of three log forts.
bodyMarkdown:
Before there was an [Elizabethtown](https://grokipedia.com/page/Elizabethtown,_Kentucky), there was Severns Valley, named for John Severns, an explorer and surveyor who likely came through in the late 1770s.

Exploring parties built cabins in 1779. Permanent settlement began in the spring of 1780, when families from Virginia and Pennsylvania came through a hard winter to make homes in the valley.

## Three forts

The newcomers settled in the middle of a war. Native nations were fighting American settlement in Kentucky, and the settlers feared raids. Three leaders, Samuel Haycraft Sr., Captain Thomas Helm and Colonel Andrew Hynes, built log forts that formed a defensive triangle.

The danger lasted for years. Grokipedia's Elizabethtown article says attacks went on until 1794, when the [Battle of Fallen Timbers](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Fallen_Timbers) reduced fighting in the region. (The article calls it a treaty. Fallen Timbers was a battle, and the peace treaty followed at Greenville in 1795.)

## A county and its name

[Hardin County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hardin_County,_Kentucky) was created on December 15, 1792, from part of Nelson County. It was named for Colonel [John Hardin](/stories/col-john-hardin-of-pleasant-run/), a Revolutionary War officer killed that year while on a peace mission to Native nations in Ohio. Hardin had earlier fought in the campaigns described in [Little Turtle and Hardin's Defeat](/stories/little-turtle-and-hardins-defeat-1790/).

The new county was named for him within months of his death.

## A town for Elizabeth

In 1793, Andrew Hynes surveyed a 30-acre tract that had been known as Severns Station. On July 4, 1797, the town was formally established on that land, which Hynes donated. He named it for his wife, Elizabeth Scarborough Hynes. Elizabethtown became the seat of Hardin County.

The town also has a link to the Lincoln family. Sarah Bush Johnston was born in the area in 1788. On December 2, 1819, she married the widower Thomas Lincoln in Elizabethtown and became stepmother to Abraham Lincoln, then ten years old.

## Kentucky today

Elizabethtown is now the seat of Hardin County, with an estimated 34,565 people in July 2024. It lies along Interstate 65 between Louisville and Bowling Green, near Fort Knox, which remains the area's largest employer. The modern city grew from a valley named for an explorer, a triangle of forts and a 30-acre gift named for Elizabeth Hynes.
